text: Every test so far deployed a brand-new contract into an empty EVM. That's fine for unit logic, but your real contract is going to call into Uniswap pools with billions in liquidity, read Chainlink price feeds, and interact with tokens that have weird transfer behavior. None of that exists in a fresh deployment.

Fork testing runs your tests against a local EVM that's an exact copy of real chain state at a given block. Pinning fork-block-number makes the test reproducible — the exact same real-world state every time you run it, instead of whatever mainnet looks like right now, which would make a failing test impossible to debug reliably later.

Cross-chain contracts need to test interactions between different chains in a single test function. vm.createFork and vm.selectFork let a test hold multiple forks and switch between them — selecting the mainnet fork to read one balance, then switching to the optimism fork to read another, all inside the same test.

If both fork-url and fork-block-number are specified, Forge caches the fetched state for that block locally, so the second and subsequent runs read from disk instead of re-querying your RPC provider. If a provider starts rate-limiting fork requests, fork-retry-backoff adds exponential backoff instead of the suite just failing outright.

Fork testing is how Chapter 3's multi-chain deployments actually get verified before mainnet, not just unit-tested in isolation. You're ready for Lesson 5 once you can explain why pinning a fork to a specific block number matters for reproducibility.
